levels.title: Name the Parts
levels.story: In a hollow of Wordwood, Wren has pinned a label on every word: this one is a thing, this one is an action. "Tagging," says Wren. "Do it by hand for a day and you'll see why a program struggles with it."

everyday.scene: A voice assistant hears 'book a table' and 'read this book'. The first 'book' is a verb and the second is a noun, and the right answer depends on it.
everyday.question: Why does a program need to know whether a word is a noun or a verb?
everyday.answer: The job of a word changes its meaning and how it should be handled. Labelling each word with its part of speech is the first step towards understanding a sentence.

lessons.title: Labelling every word
text: Part-of-speech tagging gives each word in a sentence a label for its job: noun, verb, adjective, determiner and so on. In 'a sleepy owl watches', the tags are determiner, adjective, noun, verb.
Tag sets differ. Some are very fine and some use only a handful of tags. We use four plain ones: NOUN for things, VERB for actions, ADJ for describing words, and DET for words like 'a' and 'the'.

lessons.title: One word, two tags
text: Tagging is harder than looking words up, because many words can have more than one tag. 'Duck' can be a bird or an action. 'Can' can be 'is able to' or a tin.

A simple tagger gives each word the tag it had most often in a tagged text. The table shows made-up counts from a small tagged text. It works for many words but fails when the less common job is the one in use.

references.title: NLTK book, chapter 5: Categorizing and Tagging Words

lessons.title: Let the neighbours help
text: Neighbouring words give strong clues. After 'the' or 'a', a noun or adjective is likely. After 'can', a verb is likely. 'The duck can duck' reads sensibly because 'can' signals a verb next.

text.text: Better taggers use these clues. Some are built on hidden Markov models, which count how often tags follow one another and use those counts to pick a tag for a word in context. The next level covers them.

activities.prompt: In 'A sleepy owl watches the quiet wood', what is each word?
hints: Nouns name things. Verbs name actions.
Describing words sit before the noun they describe.
activities.explain: 'A' and 'the' are determiners, 'sleepy' and 'quiet' describe, 'owl' and 'wood' are things, and 'watches' is the action.

activities.prompt: 'Duck' was a noun 8 times out of 10. What percentage of the time was it a noun?
Watch a baseline tagger work through a sentence.
activities.explain: The baseline picks each word's most common tag. It gets 3 out of 4 right here, and misses on the less common use of 'duck'.

steps.say: Sentence: 'the duck can duck'. A baseline tagger gives each word the tag it had most often in a small tagged text. Each box will show the tag it picks.
'The' was tagged DET (a determiner) all 20 times in the text. The baseline says DET, and that is right.
'Duck' was a noun 8 times and a verb 2 times, so the baseline says NOUN. In this sentence the first 'duck' is the bird, so that is right.

predict.prompt: 'Duck' was a noun 8 times and a verb 2 times. What tag does the baseline give it?
hints: Pick the tag it had more often.

steps.say: 'Can' was a verb 6 times and a noun 4 times, so the baseline says VERB. Here it means 'is able to', so that is right again.
The last 'duck' is something the bird can do: crouch. It is a verb here, but the baseline still says NOUN because that is its most common tag. One mistake in four words.

predict.prompt: The baseline tagged 3 of 4 words correctly. What is its accuracy on this sentence?
hints: Divide correct words by total words.

fieldNotes.title: Why tagging is hard
fieldNotes.text: Part-of-speech tagging is harder than looking up words, because some words can represent more than one part of speech at different times.

fieldNotes.title: Many tag sets
fieldNotes.text: Tag sets vary: some systems use many fine-grained tags, and others use a smaller number.

fieldNotes.title: Why tags help
fieldNotes.text: Word classes such as nouns and verbs are useful categories for many language processing tasks.

source.title: NLTK book, chapter 5: Categorizing and Tagging Words

summary: You gave words tags like noun and verb, saw that one word can have two tags, and watched a most-common-tag baseline get a sentence mostly right and miss the unusual use.
Wren steps back from the labelled branches. "A tag is a guess about a word's job. A good guess uses the words around it."

mistake.title: Trusting a word's usual tag
mistake.text: A word's most common tag is only a guess. The sentence around it decides which job it has this time.

levels.title: Hidden Weather
levels.story: Warden Wren lives in a cabin with no windows. Kit stands outside and watches what Wren wears each morning. "A cloak means rain, probably. A hat means sun, probably. From the clothes, can you guess the weather I can't see?"

everyday.scene: A friend says 'I'm fine' in a flat voice, and you suspect they are not. You are guessing something hidden, their mood, from something you can see, their voice.
everyday.question: How can you work out the most likely hidden story behind a row of clues?
everyday.answer: Give each hidden possibility a chance, work out how likely each clue is under each one, and find the best chain. That is the idea behind a hidden Markov model.

lessons.title: Hidden and seen
text: A hidden Markov model, or HMM, has hidden states you cannot see and observations you can. The weather is hidden. Wren's clothes are seen. Two sets of chances drive it: transitions, how one hidden state follows another, and emissions, how likely each sight is in each state.
In tagging, the hidden states are parts of speech and the observations are the words. The model asks which chain of tags best explains the sentence.

terms.meaning: Something the model cannot observe, like the weather.
Something it can see, like Wren's clothes.

lessons.title: Scoring one path
text: One guess for three days, such as Rainy, Sunny, Sunny, gets a score. Multiply the chance of the first state, the chance of the first clue in it, then for each later day the chance of moving to the next state and of its clue.
For cloak, hat, hat: 0.4 x 0.6 for day one, 0.3 x 0.6 for day two and 0.8 x 0.6 for day three. The product is about 0.0207. Rainy, Rainy, Rainy scores only 0.0012.

predict.prompt: Starting chances are 0.4 for Rainy and 0.6 for Sunny. A cloak has chance 0.6 in rain. What is the score for starting Rainy and seeing a cloak?

lessons.title: Finding the best path
text: With 2 states over 3 days there are 8 possible paths, and over 10 days there are 1,024. Checking each one does not scale. The Viterbi algorithm keeps just the best score reaching each state on each day, and then traces back.
That is dynamic programming: store the best partial answers and build on them. It gives the single most likely path of hidden states.

text.text: An HMM tagger runs the same steps with tags as states and words as clues, and the Viterbi algorithm can find the best chain of tags.

activities.prompt: Day 1 is a cloak. Rainy starts at 0.4 and a cloak in rain has chance 0.6. What is Rainy's day-1 score?
hints: Multiply start chance by clue chance.

activities.prompt: In the weather story, is each thing hidden or seen?
hints: Kit can only see Wren's clothes.
The weather is inside the cabin's walls.
activities.explain: The weather is the hidden state. Wren's cloak and hat are what Kit can see.
On each day, Viterbi keeps the best score for each state, then traces back. The best weather chain is Rainy, Sunny, Sunny.

steps.say: Kit sees what Wren wears on three days: a cloak, then a hat, then a hat. The weather is hidden. Wren wants the most likely weather for each day.
Day 1, cloak. Rainy: start 0.4 times cloak-in-rain 0.6 is 0.24. Sunny: start 0.6 times cloak-in-sun 0.1 is 0.06.

predict.prompt: Rainy starts at 0.4, and a cloak in rain has chance 0.6. What is the day-1 score for Rainy?

steps.say: Day 2, hat. For each state, keep the best way of getting there. Sunny: from Sunny is 0.06 x 0.8 = 0.048, from Rainy is 0.24 x 0.3 = 0.072. Keep 0.072, then multiply by the hat chance 0.6 to get 0.0432. Rainy: 0.24 x 0.7 x 0.1 = 0.0168.

predict.prompt: Which state scores higher on day 2?

steps.say: Day 3, hat again. Sunny comes to 0.0432 x 0.8 x 0.6 = 0.0207. Rainy comes to 0.0168 x 0.7 x 0.1 = 0.0012. Sunny is far ahead.

predict.prompt: Which state has the best score on day 3?

steps.say: Trace back from the best final state, following which state each best score came from. The most likely weather is Rainy, Sunny, Sunny. The score is 0.0207.

activities.prompt: Score the path Rainy, Sunny, Sunny for cloak, hat, hat: 0.4 x 0.6 x 0.3 x 0.6 x 0.8 x 0.6. What is it to 4 places?
With 2 hidden states and 3 days, how many different paths are there?
activities.explain: Two choices on each of three days gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 paths.

activities.prompt: Put the Viterbi steps in order.
items: For each later day keep the best score reaching each state
Pick the best state on the last day
Trace back to find the whole path
hints: Tracing back comes at the end.
activities.explain: Score day 1, then each later day keeping the best way to reach each state, pick the best final state and trace back.

fieldNotes.title: Hidden Markov models
fieldNotes.text: A hidden Markov model describes a system whose states cannot be seen directly but produce observations that can be.

fieldNotes.title: Viterbi
fieldNotes.text: The Viterbi algorithm is a dynamic programming algorithm that finds the most likely sequence of hidden events that would explain a sequence of observed events.

fieldNotes.title: In tagging
fieldNotes.text: In part-of-speech tagging with an HMM, the hidden states are the underlying parts of speech and the observed sequence is the words.

summary: You met hidden states and observations, scored a whole path by multiplying chances, and used Viterbi to find the best chain without checking every path.
Wren peeks out of the cabin. "A cloak on day one, hats after. So rain, then sun. You were right."

mistake.title: Picking each day's best guess alone
mistake.text: The best weather for one day may not fit the best chain. Viterbi looks at the whole sequence so each guess agrees with its neighbours.
